title: Cardiac Arrhythmias
subject: Medicine
summary: Arrhythmias are disturbances of heart rhythm that can be benign or life‑threatening. Recognising patterns, underlying causes and appropriate urgent actions is essential, especially where diagnostics are limited.

sections.p: An arrhythmia is any deviation from the normal sinus rhythm in rate, regularity, or conduction. Diagnosis is made by pulse assessment and ECG, looking for rate, rhythm, QRS width and axis.
b: Sinus rhythm: regular, rate 60‑100, P‑QRS‑T sequence
Bradycardia: <60 bpm, may be symptomatic
Tachycardia: >100 bpm, classify narrow vs wide QRS

sections.p: Severity is judged by haemodynamic impact and risk of degeneration to ventricular fibrillation.
b: Stable: normal blood pressure, no chest pain, no syncope
Unstable: hypotension, altered mental status, acute heart failure, chest pain
Life‑threatening: pulseless ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation

sections.p: Identify precipitating factors; in low‑resource settings infectious and metabolic triggers are common.
b: Electrolyte disturbances – hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia
Ischaemic heart disease – acute MI, chronic coronary disease
Infections – malaria, HIV‑related myocarditis, TB pericarditis
Drug‑induced – quinine, anti‑arrhythmics, herbal stimulants
Structural heart disease – rheumatic valve disease, cardiomyopathy, sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with palpitations, dizziness, syncope, chest pain or heart failure signs.
b: Palpitations: awareness of irregular beats
Syncope/presyncope: sudden drop in cerebral perfusion
Dyspnoea: due to reduced cardiac output or heart failure
Chest discomfort: especially with ischaemic tachyarrhythmias

t.b: What rhythm is present and is there evidence of ischaemia or electrolyte effect?
Is there myocardial injury driving the arrhythmia?
Is there evidence of heart enlargement, pulmonary oedema or TB?
Is there pericardial effusion or severe ventricular dysfunction?

sections.p: Prompt recognition of instability prevents sudden cardiac death.
b: Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) with arrhythmia
Altered consciousness or seizures
Chest pain suggestive of acute MI
Signs of heart failure – pulmonary crackles, peripheral oedema

sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, stabilise the patient, then apply rhythm‑specific therapy.
b: Immediate: oxygen, IV access, monitor, treat reversible causes (e.g., replace K+ if <3.3 mmol/L)
Tachyarrhythmias with instability → synchronized cardioversion (100 J for SVT, 200 J for VT)
Stable narrow‑complex SVT → vagal maneuvers, then adenosine if available; avoid beta‑blockers in acute asthma
Stable wide‑complex VT → amiodarone infusion; avoid class IC drugs in structural heart disease
Long‑term: beta‑blockers for rate control in AF, anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂‑VASc ≥2, consider rhythm control if symptomatic

sections.p: Arrange outpatient review within 1 week for persistent arrhythmia or after discharge from an unstable episode.
b: Educate on avoiding stimulants, correcting electrolyte imbalance, and adherence to malaria prophylaxis or HIV therapy
Screen for underlying structural disease with echocardiography when feasible
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce cardiac stress

sections.p: Distinguish arrhythmias from other causes of palpitations or syncope.
b: Premature beats (PVCs/PACs) – isolated, usually benign
Anxiety‑related tachycardia – normal sinus rhythm, no ECG abnormalities
Orthostatic hypotension – drop in BP on standing, not rhythm disturbance

sections.p: Certain findings may mask the severity of an arrhythmia.
b: Normal potassium in a patient on diuretics may hide intracellular depletion; check Mg2+
A ‘normal’ ECG taken after a brief episode may miss paroxysmal AF; consider Holter or event monitor
Low‑grade fever can be misattributed to infection while the real trigger is electrolyte loss

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid wide‑complex tachycardia (>150 bpm) causing breathlessness

faq.q: Why is hypokalaemia dangerous in arrhythmias?
faq.a: Low K+ prolongs repolarisation, creating early after‑depolarisation and predisposes to ventricular tachycardia.

faq.q: When is cardioversion preferred over drugs?
faq.a: When the patient is haemodynamically unstable or when rapid restoration of sinus rhythm is needed.

faq.q: Can atrial fibrillation be managed without anticoagulation?
faq.a: Only if the CHA₂DS₂‑VASc score is 0 (men) or 1 (women); otherwise anticoagulation is required to prevent stroke.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with palpitations and a pulse of 130 bpm – what is your immediate assessment and why? — Check haemodynamic stability, obtain ECG, correct electrolytes; malaria can cause hypokalaemia precipitating SVT.

You see a regular wide‑complex tachycardia at 180 bpm in a patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis – what is the most likely rhythm and next step? — Likely ventricular tachycardia; if unstable, immediate synchronized cardioversion.

A patient on quinine for severe malaria develops a new irregular pulse; ECG shows absent P waves and irregularly irregular QRS – what is the diagnosis and management? — New‑onset atrial fibrillation; control rate with digoxin (avoid beta‑blocker if bronchospasm) and assess anticoagulation need.
Why is adenosine contraindicated in a patient with asthma presenting with SVT? — Adenosine can cause bronchospasm; use vagal maneuvers or calcium channel blocker instead.

Explain how you would differentiate between a PVC and ventricular tachycardia on a limited ECG strip. — PVCs are isolated, have a compensatory pause; VT shows a series of wide QRS complexes without normal beats.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden tachycardia and chest pain; ECG is normal. What non‑cardiac cause should you consider? — Acute pain crisis causing sympathetic surge; treat pain and reassess rhythm.
When is a trans‑cutaneous pacemaker indicated in bradyarrhythmia? — When symptomatic bradycardia persists despite atropine and the patient is unstable.

What electrolyte abnormality is most likely to cause a peaked T wave and how does it affect arrhythmia risk? — Hyperkalaemia (>5.5 mmol/L) shortens repolarisation, leading to peaked T waves and risk of ventricular fibrillation.
